screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts: Reading Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn how your DApp reads on-chain state without creating transactions. Contract object, call read-only functions marked view or pure using the. call() helper, and handle returned values such as uint256 that Web3. js typically presents as strings. Reading is safe and gas-free when done correctly, but there are common pitfalls: wrong ABI or address, forgetting to await Promises, and misinterpreting numeric types. Ask yourself after each example: am I using the right ABI, address, and. call() for a read-only operation?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Interacting with Smart Contracts: Reading Data
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Read-only contract calls with Web3.js

Learn how ABI and address let your DApp request data, why .call() is gas-free, and how to present results safely to users.

ABI
JSON description of contract functions and types used to encode and decode calls.
Address
Deployed contract's unique hexadecimal identifier on the network.
Contract Instance
A web3.eth.Contract object that exposes .methods and lets you call functions.
Orientation

You'll follow a small live-coding flow: compile SimpleStorage, obtain ABI and address, instantiate the contract in app.js, then call getNumber and add using .call(). We'll also show how to safely convert returned values for display.

Why it matters
Read operations power UI data: balances, metadata, and game state without costing gas.
Common error
Using the wrong ABI or forgetting await will cause confusing errors or unresolved Promises.
Visual concept
ABI JSON
Function signatures, inputs, outputs, mutability
Contract Address
Deployed on the network after migration
.call()
Executes view/pure functions locally — no gas or mining required
Explore Key Topics
ABI & Address
The minimum required info to build a contract instance in Web3.js.
Read-only calls
Use .call() to query state or compute results without transactions.
Numeric handling
Expect uint256 as strings; convert with parseInt or BigInt/BN when needed.

screens.title: What is the ABI and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: The Application Binary Interface, or ABI, is the JSON description that tells Web3. js how to encode calls to a smart contract and decode the returned data. Think of the ABI as the contract's public contract: it lists every function name, the types and names of parameters, the return types, and flags like view, pure, or nonpayable. This information is generated by the Solidity compiler when you build a contract. Without the ABI, your DApp cannot form correct method calls — Web3. js would not know how to serialize parameters or parse results. For example, the SimpleStorage ABI includes entries for getNumber and add, describing that add takes two uint256 parameters and returns a uint256. A common misconception is that the contract address alone is sufficient; it is not. The address locates the code on-chain, but the ABI is the map to interpret that code's functions and results. In practice you keep ABI JSON with your frontend build artifacts and update it whenever you change contract interfaces. Key takeaway: always ship the matching ABI for the deployed contract version. Check that the ABI's function names and parameter order match the deployed bytecode's expectations before calling any method.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › ABI Explained
Definition

Application Binary Interface

A machine-readable JSON array that lists a contract's public functions, inputs, outputs, and mutability so tooling like Web3.js can interact with it.

Example
An ABI entry for add shows it accepts two uint256 inputs and returns a uint256; Web3 uses that to encode parameters and decode the sum.
Mnemonic
ABI = function map; think of it as the contract's public API schema.
Why this matters
  • Web3.js relies on the ABI to form method calls and decode returned values.
  • A mismatched ABI can cause cryptic errors or incorrect return parsing.
  • Keep the ABI in your frontend build artifacts and update it when you recompile contracts.
Common mistake
Using an ABI from a different contract version. Even minor signature changes break call encoding.
Key takeaway
Always ship and reference the ABI that matches your deployed contract bytecode.

screens.title: Contract Address: the location on-chain
screens.narratorSegment: A contract address is the unique on-chain location where a contract's bytecode and storage live. After a successful deployment you receive a hexadecimal address; this address is how Web3. js knows where to direct encoded calls. The address alone is not enough: address locates the code, ABI tells you how to talk to that code. A simple analogy is a restaurant directory: the address gets you to the building, the menu (ABI) tells you what to order and what to expect back. A common misconception is that any ABI will work with any address on the same network; in reality the ABI must correspond to the specific compiled contract at that address. For example, after deploying SimpleStorage on a local Ganache instance you'll copy the deployment address and use it together with the SimpleStorage ABI in new web3. eth. Contract(simpleStorageABI, contractAddress). If you accidentally use an address from another contract or the wrong network, calls will fail or return unexpected values. Key takeaway: always confirm both network and address when instantiating a contract instance in your DApp. Contract Address: the location on-chain means the contract address identifies deployed code; it must be used with the matching abi and correct network to form successful calls.. In practical terms, why address and abi are both required to interact with a contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Contract Address
Definition

Contract Address

A unique hexadecimal address assigned when a contract is deployed. It points to the contract's code and storage on a specific network.

Example
After deploying SimpleStorage to Ganache you might see an address like 0x5FbDB2... Use that exact string when creating a new web3.eth.Contract instance.
Checklist
  • Confirm network (Ganache, Sepolia, etc.).
  • Copy address from deployment receipt or explorer.
  • Use the address with the matching ABI in your frontend.
Common mistake
Using an address from a different network or contract leads to failures or unexpected values.
Key takeaway
Always verify both network and deployed address before instantiating a Contract object.

screens.title: Instantiating web3.eth.Contract
screens.narratorSegment: To interact with contract functions from your frontend you must create a Contract instance. In Web3. js this is done with new web3. eth. Contract(contractABI, contractAddress). The contractABI is the JSON array produced by the Solidity compiler and contractAddress is the deployed address string. Once instantiated, the object exposes a. methods property that mirrors the contract's public functions. For example, with SimpleStorage you get simpleStorageContract. methods. getNumber() and simpleStorageContract. methods. add(a,b). To make this concrete, the loadContract function should check web3 is initialized, then assign simpleStorageContract = new web3. eth. Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageContractAddress). A common error is attempting to access. methods before the instance is created, so guard your code and only call methods after loadContract completes. Also ensure the ABI you pass exactly matches the compiled contract; otherwise encoding or decoding may fail. Example code is shown in the visual panel. Key takeaway: creating a Contract instance is a local setup step that translates your ABI and address into callable JavaScript methods backed by the connected node. Instantiating web3.eth.Contract means use new web3.eth.contract(abi, address) after web3 is initialized; then call functions through the .methods property.. In practical terms, create a contract instance with abi and address to access .methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Instantiate Contract
Code Walkthrough

Create the Contract instance

const simpleStorageABI = [ /* your ABI JSON array */ ];
const simpleStorageContractAddress = '0xYourDeployedContractAddressHere';
let simpleStorageContract;

async function loadContract() {
  if (!web3) {
    console.error('Web3 not initialized');
    return;
  }
  simpleStorageContract = new web3.eth.Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageContractAddress);
  console.log('Contract instance loaded:', simpleStorageContract);
}
Tip
Load the contract after wallet connection so web3 is ready.
Pitfall
Referencing .methods before initialization returns undefined behavior.
How it works
  • ABI tells Web3 how to encode function calls.
  • Address tells Web3 where to send encoded messages.
  • The Contract object exposes .methods.() to call functions.
Key takeaway
Instantiate after web3 is available and keep ABI/address in your frontend config.

screens.title: Calling view and pure functions with .call()
screens.narratorSegment: Calling a read-only function follows a consistent three-step flow: reference the instanced contract, call the method with parameters, and await the result. First, ensure your contract instance exists: if simpleStorageContract is undefined, load it and only then continue. Second, use the. methods property with the function name and arguments, for example simpleStorageContract. methods. getNumber(). call() for a view function or simpleStorageContract. methods. add(5,7). call() for a pure function. Third, await the Promise returned by. call(), then use the resolved value to update your UI. Remember. call() executes locally on the connected node, so it does not create a broadcast transaction or consume gas. A concrete example: const storedNumber = await simpleStorageContract. methods. getNumber(). call(); then set textContent of a display element to storedNumber. Common misconceptions include forgetting to await, which logs a Promise object instead of the value, or expecting. call() to change state — it cannot. Key takeaway: treat. call() as an asynchronous read operation that returns resolved values you can safely render in your DApp. Calling view and pure functions with .call() means ensure contract is loaded, use .methods.fn(args).call(), await its promise, and then update the ui with the returned value.. In practical terms, step-by-step: build the method call, await the promise, and update ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Calling .call()
Process

Three-step read-only call

1. Ensure Contract is loaded
Do not call methods before new web3.eth.Contract(...) has completed.
2. Use .methods and call()
Example: await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
3. Await and render
Update DOM elements with the resolved value and handle errors.
Concrete example
// call a view function
const storedNumber = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
document.getElementById('displayNumber').textContent = storedNumber;
Misconception
.call() does not and cannot modify contract state. To change state you must send a transaction with .send() and pay gas.
Key takeaway
Use .call() for reads, await the result, and update your UI without creating transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › getStoredNumber & add walkthrough
Code
async function getContractData() {
  if (!simpleStorageContract) {
    console.error('Contract not loaded.');
    return;
  }
  try {
    const storedNum = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
    document.getElementById('displayNumber').textContent = storedNum;

    const sumResult = await simpleStorageContract.methods.add(10, 20).call();
    document.getElementById('displaySum').textContent = sumResult;

  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error reading from contract:', error);
    document.getElementById('displayNumber').textContent = 'Error';
    document.getElementById('displaySum').textContent = 'Error';
  }
}
Note
Calls return strings for uint256; use parseInt for small values or BN/BigInt for large ones.
Pitfall
Logging without await prints a Promise instead of the resolved value.
Example scenario
A DApp displays a stored game score and a computed bonus. Use getNumber().call() for the score and add(base,bonus).call() for the computed value, then show both on the page.
Key takeaway
Wrap calls in try/catch, await them, update UI, and choose proper numeric conversion strategy.

screens.title: view vs pure vs transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity functions fall into categories that determine how you interact with them. view functions can read contract state but cannot modify it; they are ideal for reading persistent values like stored variables. pure functions do not read or modify contract state — they operate entirely on parameters and return computed values. Both view and pure functions can be invoked from the frontend using. call(), which executes locally on a node and costs no gas. In contrast, functions that alter state (nonpayable or payable) require transactions submitted with. send() or similar and will consume gas and require mining. A common misconception is thinking. call() will update state or that. call() and. send() are interchangeable. Use. call() for queries and dry-run computations, and use transactions for state-changing operations. Comparison
view

pure

screens.title: uint256 results and numeric handling
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum numeric types like uint256 can exceed JavaScript's safe integer range, so Web3. js returns them as strings by default to avoid precision loss. When you call a view or pure function that returns a uint256, you'll typically receive a string such as "12345678901234567890". For small values you can safely use parseInt(value, 10) to convert to a JavaScript Number for display or lightweight arithmetic. For larger values or production arithmetic you should use BigInt or the Web3. js BN utilities: web3. utils. toBN(value) or BigInt(value) to perform exact math. A common mistake is converting huge values to Number and losing precision, which leads to incorrect calculations and possible security issues if financial logic depends on exact amounts. If your token uses 18 decimals, you'll also need to apply a conversion like web3. utils. fromWei(rawBalance, 'ether') before showing a human-readable amount. Key takeaway: treat returned uint256 strings carefully and choose an appropriate numeric type for arithmetic or display. uint256 results and numeric handling means web3.js returns uint256 as strings. use parseint for small numbers, bigint or web3.utils.tobn for large integers, and fromwei or decimals conversion for token units.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Handling uint256

Returned integers as strings

Web3.js returns large integers as strings to avoid JavaScript precision loss. Convert depending on expected size and use-case.

Small number
parseInt(storedNumber, 10) is fine for values well within Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
Large number
Use web3.utils.toBN(value) or BigInt(value) for precise arithmetic.
Token decimals
If a balance uses 18 decimals, apply web3.utils.fromWei(rawBalance, 'ether') for user-friendly display.
Code examples
// small number
const n = parseInt(storedNumber, 10);

// big number with BN
const bn = web3.utils.toBN(storedNumber);

// display wei as ether
const readable = web3.utils.fromWei(rawBalance, 'ether');
Key takeaway
Do not coerce large uint256 values to Number; use BN or BigInt and convert units when needed for display.

screens.title: Common pitfalls when calling read-only functions
screens.narratorSegment: When calling read-only contract functions you will encounter several recurring mistakes. First, using an incorrect ABI or address causes calls to fail or return nonsense; always verify the ABI matches the deployed code and the address matches the intended deployment and network. Second, forgetting to await the Promise returned by. call() leads to logging unresolved Promises or attempting to use values before they exist; always use await or. then(). Third, misinterpreting return types — especially uint256 — is common: treat them as strings and convert with parseInt for small numbers or BN/BigInt for larger arithmetic. Fourth, attempting to change state with. call() is a logical error;. call() never alters blockchain state. Fifth, not handling RPC errors or network disconnects will result in poor UX; wrap calls in try/catch and show clear error states in the UI. Finally, for token balances remember to account for decimals when presenting values to users. Key takeaway: validate ABI and address, await calls, handle numeric types properly, and always handle errors gracefully. async function getContractData() {

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn how your DApp reads on-chain state without creating transactions. You will see why the ABI and the deployed contract address are the two essential ingredients Web3. js needs to speak to a smart contract. We'll instantiate a web3. eth. Contract object, call read-only functions marked view or pure using the. call() helper, and handle returned values such as uint256 that Web3. js typically presents as strings. Reading is safe and gas-free when done correctly, but there are common pitfalls: wrong ABI or address, forgetting to await Promises, and misinterpreting numeric types. Throughout these screens you'll get concrete code examples — both Solidity and JavaScript — a hands-on activity to wire an index. html and app. js, and quick checks so you can fetch and show values like a stored number or a computed sum. By the end you'll be able to connect a wallet, load a Contract instance, run getNumber and add from SimpleStorage, and display the results in your UI with correct numeric handling. Ask yourself after each example: am I using the right ABI, address, and. call() for a read-only operation?

Our core learning goals focus on practical contract reads that power user interfaces. First, you'll understand the Application Binary Interface and why it is required to encode function calls and decode return values. The ABI is a JSON description produced by the compiler; without it Web3. js cannot form correct method calls. Second, you'll know how to create a web3. eth. Contract instance using the ABI and the contract's deployed address. This instance exposes. methods that map to your Solidity functions and events. Third, you'll be able to call Solidity functions declared view or pure using the. call() pattern; these execute locally on a node and don't create a transaction or cost gas. Fourth, you'll learn to process returned values — especially uint256 — which Web3. js commonly returns as strings, and you'll convert them for UI display safely. Each objective is accompanied by a competency milestone so you can verify your progress. Throughout, examples use a SimpleStorage contract to make outcomes concrete. Practice by fetching getNumber and calling add with literal inputs, then show both results in the page. Notice how these read operations let your DApp stay responsive and transparent to users.

These milestone cards turn objectives into practical tasks you can complete in your project. First milestone: compile SimpleStorage and confirm an ABI file exists — open the compiler output and inspect the JSON types array to see function signatures. Second milestone: deploy and capture the contract address; paste it into your app. js and confirm the address matches the deployed transaction receipt. Third milestone: instantiate web3. eth. Contract and call getNumber with. call() and await the Promise; you should see a string in the console rather than a Promise object. Fourth milestone: implement a UI element that shows both the stored number and a computed sum from add(a,b), and add a refresh button that re-fetches values without sending a transaction. If you can complete these steps, you've connected wallet, created a Contract instance, executed read-only calls, and handled returned numeric strings safely. Each milestone includes a simple visual mnemonic and a verification hint so you can check your work quickly in the browser console or page elements.

The Application Binary Interface, or ABI, is the JSON description that tells Web3. js how to encode calls to a smart contract and decode the returned data. Think of the ABI as the contract's public contract: it lists every function name, the types and names of parameters, the return types, and flags like view, pure, or nonpayable. This information is generated by the Solidity compiler when you build a contract. Without the ABI, your DApp cannot form correct method calls — Web3. js would not know how to serialize parameters or parse results. For example, the SimpleStorage ABI includes entries for getNumber and add, describing that add takes two uint256 parameters and returns a uint256. A common misconception is that the contract address alone is sufficient; it is not. The address locates the code on-chain, but the ABI is the map to interpret that code's functions and results. In practice you keep ABI JSON with your frontend build artifacts and update it whenever you change contract interfaces. Key takeaway: always ship the matching ABI for the deployed contract version. Check that the ABI's function names and parameter order match the deployed bytecode's expectations before calling any method.

A contract address is the unique on-chain location where a contract's bytecode and storage live. After a successful deployment you receive a hexadecimal address; this address is how Web3. js knows where to direct encoded calls. The address alone is not enough: address locates the code, ABI tells you how to talk to that code. A simple analogy is a restaurant directory: the address gets you to the building, the menu (ABI) tells you what to order and what to expect back. A common misconception is that any ABI will work with any address on the same network; in reality the ABI must correspond to the specific compiled contract at that address. For example, after deploying SimpleStorage on a local Ganache instance you'll copy the deployment address and use it together with the SimpleStorage ABI in new web3. eth. Contract(simpleStorageABI, contractAddress). If you accidentally use an address from another contract or the wrong network, calls will fail or return unexpected values. Key takeaway: always confirm both network and address when instantiating a contract instance in your DApp. Contract Address: the location on-chain means the contract address identifies deployed code; it must be used with the matching abi and correct network to form successful calls.. In practical terms, why address and abi are both required to interact with a contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Solidity functions fall into categories that determine how you interact with them. view functions can read contract state but cannot modify it; they are ideal for reading persistent values like stored variables. pure functions do not read or modify contract state — they operate entirely on parameters and return computed values. In contrast, functions that alter state (nonpayable or payable) require transactions submitted with. send() or similar and will consume gas and require mining.
